reports.name: Pete Crow-Armstrong
reports.published_report: The tension in the profile is that the contact profile and the power profile are pointing in opposite directions. His xSLG sits at .467 and his Hard-Hit rate is 48.5%, both well above average, but his xBA is exactly league average at .250 and his 33.9% Chase rate ranks in just the 23rd percentile. He's getting to good contact less often than the damage he does suggests he should. What saves the profile is the walk rate: 11.7% BB pulls the overall value back up, and the sprint speed at 29.5 ft/s adds a dimension most hitters with this kind of chase rate can't lean on. If the chase rate stays where it is and the strikeout rate holds near 27.2%, the projection's .270/.362/.516 line is the ceiling holding, not a conservative floor — you're buying the speed and the hard contact carrying a real discipline problem.

reports.name: Shohei Ohtani

reports.name: James Wood
reports.published_report: The contact risk is documented and it isn't shrinking — 28.6% strikeouts, a whiff rate in the 16th percentile, and none of that is going away. What makes Wood so hard to dismiss is that the contact he does make is essentially maxed out: 95.1 mph average exit velocity at the 100th percentile, a 20.8% barrel rate also at the 100th, and an xSLG of .585 that describes a hitter who does catastrophic damage when he connects. Layer in a 16.8% walk rate that almost no hitters in the league match, and the .419 xwOBA tells you the strikeouts are a tax, not a ceiling. If it holds, you get something close to the projected .264/.388/.526 line with 36 home runs across 656 plate appearances; if the strikeout rate climbs further, the walks and raw power are still enough to carry a plus offensive profile.

reports.name: A.J. Ewing
reports.published_report: The 26.5% chase rate is the best thing about this profile, and the 25.7% strikeout rate is the worst. Both live in the same hitter, which is genuinely uncomfortable: he reads spin well enough to lay off but still whiffs often enough inside the zone that the contact quality, a .326 xwOBA sitting right around league average, never fully capitalizes on the discipline. What rescues the overall picture is 29.4 ft/s sprint speed, a genuine weapon that inflates the value of every .251 average and every 23 projected stolen bases into something a flat slash line undersells. If the strikeout rate finds a lower gear, the chase discipline is already there to build on, and the speed gives him a floor as a useful outfield piece regardless; if it doesn't, he's a fast, average bat who will need the glove, which the 90th-percentile OAA suggests he can supply.

reports.name: Termarr Johnson
reports.published_report: The walk rate is the loudest thing in this profile, and also the most complicated. At AAA in 2026, Termarr Johnson has drawn 68 walks against 101 strikeouts across 406 plate appearances, and that 17% walk rate translates to 13.1% at the MLB level, where most hitters sit around 8.5%. The power, though, is a different story: his .120 ISO at AAA translates to .114 in the majors, well short of the .150 MLB average, and a .199 average sitting on a .259 BABIP suggests the contact isn't beating defenders when it lands. The 24 stolen bases at AAA matter here, because if the legs can manufacture value that the bat isn't yet providing, the floor stays livable, but everything hinges on whether the contact quality catches up enough to make opposing pitchers respect the plate discipline instead of just pitching around it. Right now the ceiling is a bench or platoon bat, and the floor is the same.

reports.name: Xavier Isaac
reports.published_report: The walk rate is the whole argument. At AA in 403 plate appearances, Xavier Isaac has drawn 77 walks against 111 strikeouts, and when that translates, it comes out to 14.1% — more than five percentage points clear of what the average big-leaguer posts. The .412 OBP and 23 home runs at AA are the headline, but the translated ISO of .182 says the power carries alongside the eye, and the average MLB hitter sits at .150. The ceiling here is a bench or platoon bat, because first base at 22 limits the floor upside more than the bat does, and everything hinges on whether that 28% strikeout rate at AA blooms into something uglier against big-league velocity, because if it does the walk rate alone won't be enough.

reports.name: Emerson Hancock
reports.published_report: The walk rate carries this entire profile. At 6.2%, Hancock sits at the 85th percentile in BB%, and when you strip away the noise, that's the one thing separating him from a thoroughly ordinary mid-rotation arm — his xERA sits at 3.97, his K% at 23.1% lands right at the median, and his chase rate at 28.1% is genuinely soft. The 95.4 mph fastball with 2355 rpm gives him a weapon, but hitters are making hard contact when they do connect, a 41.1% hard-hit rate that explains why the projection leans on command doing the heavy lifting. If the walk rate stays where it is, 167.5 innings of 3.54 ERA ball is a real outcome; if it creeps back toward average, what's left is a guy who doesn't miss enough bats to compensate.

reports.name: Cooper Ingle
reports.published_report: The .429 OBP and 18 home runs in 353 AAA plate appearances this season are genuine, and the translation is what makes this complicated. Cooper Ingle's walk rate translates to 13.5% at the MLB level, well above where the average big-leaguer lands, and a left-handed catcher with that kind of plate discipline is a legitimately scarce commodity. But the ISO translates to .189 at the MLB level, the strikeout rate edges just above league average, and the ceiling reads as a bench or platoon bat, not a regular, so the question isn't whether he can hit but whether the role he fits has enough value to matter behind the plate for Cleveland. If the contact holds and the walk rate survives the jump, he's a useful big-league catcher; if the K rate climbs and the BABIP cools from .361, the bat profile shrinks toward organizational depth fast.

reports.name: Slade Cecconi

reports.name: Nasim Nuñez
reports.published_report: Fifty projected stolen bases on a .270 xwOBA is the whole profile in two numbers, and the tension is obvious. The contact quality is essentially bottom-of-the-barrel: 84.9 mph average exit velocity, a 0.4% barrel rate, an xSLG of .271 that sits at the first percentile among hitters with enough batted balls to qualify. What saves him is that he doesn't sell out chasing — a 25.3% chase rate and 10.8% walk rate keep him on base often enough that the projected .312 OBP doesn't look absurd given the underlying plate discipline. The entire value proposition is that 29.7 ft/s sprint speed, which ranks at the 97th percentile, converts into baserunning damage that the bat could never produce on its own; if that speed ages even slightly or a team starts limiting his attempts, what's left is a bat-last middle infielder whose glove (91st percentile OAA) is the only other reason to keep running him out.

His 28% K% at AAA becomes 26.9% in MLB context, well above where the average big-leaguer lands, and 92 strikeouts in 333 plate appearances at AAA is a real number that follows him everywhere. What makes the profile livable is that the power and the walk rate are both legitimate load-bearers: a .209 ISO and 45 walks in those same 333 plate appearances, with his translated walk rate of 10.9% sitting above the MLB mean of 8.5%. The 21 stolen bases are the piece that matters most for how his floor plays out, because a bench bat who can run and take a walk earns roster spots his bat alone might not, and if the strikeout rate softens even a little, there's a low-end everyday player here rather than just a platoon piece.

reports.name: Adrian Morejon
reports.published_report: That 1.8% barrel rate is almost impossible to sustain — until you look at a 37.5% chase rate and a 34.1% whiff rate backing it up. Morejon isn't suppressing hard contact by luck; hitters are regularly swinging at pitches they can't do anything with, and 99.3 mph on the fastball is why the zone expands in his favor. The xERA sits at 2.41 and the xwOBA at .242, both in the 97th percentile, and the projection's 2.77 ERA over 82.0 innings reads as the conservative translation of a Statcast profile that has almost no weak spots. The one dependency is the walk rate, 6.6% right now, which is functional but the only lever available for opposing offenses if Morejon ever loses feel for a secondary offering.

reports.name: Troy Melton
reports.published_report: The xERA and xwOBA tell the same story: Melton suppresses hard contact at an 87th-percentile clip, and barrels allowed sit at just 5.2%, which is where the run prevention actually lives. His strikeout rate at 22.2% is roughly league average, so this isn't a swing-and-miss profile carrying him — it's the 32.9% chase rate and a fastball sitting 96.4 mph that keep hitters from squaring anything up. The whole thing hinges on whether that contact management holds over a full starter's workload, because if chase rates regress and the strikeouts don't climb to compensate, a 3.06 xERA becomes a lot harder to sustain than the projected 2.51 ERA suggests.

Jefferson Rojas is hitting .269/.338/.460 at AA with 16 home runs and 18 steals, and the MLB-equivalent ISO lands at .147, right beside the 0.15 MLB average, which tells you the power reads as functional rather than special. The whole profile hinges on whether the walk rate follows him up — at 9% in AA it translates to just 8.2%, barely a tick below the 8.5% MLB average, and if that slips any further the .338 OBP becomes a liability that exposes the ceiling. Either a bench bat with legitimate speed-and-contact value, or, if the power hardens a tick and the plate discipline stabilizes, a low-end everyday regular at third.

reports.name: Seaver King
reports.published_report: The .316/.398/.529 line across AAA & AA is loud, and the contact is what makes it worth listening to. His average translates to an MLB-equivalent that still sits near the top of the minor-league pool, but the ISO comes down to .161 in translation, basically league average power once you account for level. Everything hinges on whether the .371 BABIP reflects a genuine contact skill or just fortune, and 375 plate appearances across two levels is enough sample to take it seriously but not enough to stop asking. If the bat plays at that contact rate in the majors, he's a fringe regular at short; if the BABIP regresses and the power stays ordinary, you're looking at a bench piece.

reports.name: Connor Prielipp
reports.published_report: The fastball sits 95.6 mph and the strikeout rate clocks at 24.6%, so there's something to build on — the problem is everything around the fastball. A 9.4% walk rate and a 23.8% whiff rate don't coexist comfortably with rotation ambitions, and the contact quality when hitters do connect is genuinely rough: 41.1% hard-hit rate, average exit velocity at 90.2 mph, an xERA of 4.26 that the projection actually clears at 4.93. The profile hinges entirely on whether the command tightens enough to let the velocity play, because right now the walks are eating the strikeouts alive. If that gap closes, he's a back-end starter who gives Minnesota some innings; if it doesn't, 123 projected IP with 6 quality starts is the ceiling, not the floor.

reports.name: Bryan Reynolds
reports.published_report: The gap between an .350 xwOBA and a .248 xBA tells you exactly what Reynolds is: a quality-of-contact hitter whose actual batting average will always undersell him. He chases at just 25.2% and walks at 13.7%, which is what drives that .366 OBP projection and separates him from the typical 24.1% strikeout guy who can't compensate. The 47.0% hard-hit rate holds up the xSLG at .430 — the contact isn't soft, it's just distributed in ways that suppress hits. If the whiff rate (28.9%, bottom quarter) climbs further, the strikeouts eat into at-bats and the walk-rate magic has less room to work, but as long as discipline holds, you're looking at a legitimate everyday outfielder projecting to 703 PA of .796 OPS ball.

reports.name: Elmer Rodríguez
reports.published_report: The 2.6 ERA across 92.3 innings at AAA is loud, but the profile underneath it is more complicated than that number wants you to believe. His 94 strikeouts translate to an 8.3 K/9 in MLB terms, essentially matching what an average MLB starter posts, and his walks translate to 4.2 BB/9 when typical starters sit a full run lower. The 12% K-BB% at AAA and the MLB-equivalent 11.2% both say the same thing: the margin is thin, and he has to execute to sustain that kind of run prevention. Tighten the walks and he becomes a genuine multi-inning or setup reliever; let them stay where they are and what's left is a depth arm who needs everything else to cooperate.

reports.name: José Ramírez
reports.published_report: The Statcast profile here is genuinely unusual: a 93rd-percentile xBA of .285 sitting alongside a barrel rate of just 5.1%. He makes elite contact, with a 12.1% strikeout rate, a 13.6% walk rate, and a whiff rate in the same tier, without generating the raw thump that usually explains those expected numbers. The gap closes partly through pitch selection and bat-to-ball skill, and the projection's .247 AVG against that .285 xBA reflects the real possibility that soft-contact fortune regresses in ways his swing decisions can't prevent. What carries the profile is 38 projected steals, because speed is the multiplier that gives a .344 OBP genuine run-creation teeth even when the .410 SLG trails the xSLG.

reports.name: Brandon Lowe
reports.published_report: Thirty-two home runs in a full season is a real number for a second baseman, and the Statcast contact profile explains why it's believable and why it's uncomfortable at the same time. Exit velocity at 91.2 mph, barrels at 12.5%, hard-hit rate at 46.4%, all well above the middle of the league — the raw power is genuine. But a 35.2% whiff rate and 29.2% strikeout rate drag the xBA down to .240, which is how you get a .326 xwOBA despite all that loud contact: he hits the ball hard when he hits it, and he misses a lot. If the strikeout rate holds at that level, .249 with 32 home runs and a .469 SLG is probably close to right, a power-forward second baseman who costs you in the batting average column and gives it back in slugging.

Across AA & A+ & A in 271 plate appearances, Nimmala has drawn 37 walks against 61 strikeouts, and that 14% walk rate at 20 years old is the thing worth watching, because in MLB-equivalent terms it translates to 10.3%, a figure that clears what most big-league hitters manage. The ISO across those levels sits at .192, which sounds loud, but the translation flattens it to .143, essentially matching a typical big-leaguer's output, meaning the raw power is largely a function of the levels he's playing in rather than a true carrying tool. If the plate discipline holds and the bat-to-ball tightens even modestly, you get a shortstop who gets on base reliably; if the strikeout rate doesn't improve from where it translates, the profile thins to a bench piece with some on-base value.

reports.name: Oswald Peraza
reports.published_report: The Statcast profile here is almost entirely a discipline problem. A 38.3% chase rate and 3.8% walk rate put him at the very bottom of the league in both categories, and the contact quality, 87.6 mph average exit velocity with a .271 xwOBA, reflects what happens when a hitter is constantly defending pitches he shouldn't swing at. The 15 projected steals are genuine, sprint speed at the 82nd percentile is the one loud tool, but speed doesn't play up when you're making weak contact on bad pitches 29.4% of the time via strikeout. If the chase rate doesn't come down, the projection's .226/.276 line is the ceiling, not the floor, and he's a bench piece whose legs occasionally make a box score.

reports.name: Gage Jump
reports.published_report: The walk rate is what kills this profile. Jump sits at 96.3 mph with 2359 rpm on his fastball and punches out hitters at 25.1%, but a 10.9% walk rate undercuts almost everything good that generates — and the xERA of 4.29 reflects exactly that tradeoff. The barrel rate of 5.6% says he can miss bats when hitters do swing, but the chase rate of 30.3% means he isn't forcing many bad swings outside the zone, so the strikeouts are coming from within it, which makes the walks even more damaging. If he tightens the command, there's a mid-rotation floor in the stuff; if he doesn't, the projection's 116.6 innings at a 4.42 ERA is probably the ceiling.

That translation is the tension in this profile. The strikeout rate at AA is 26%, and once the level corrects for competition it becomes 27.3%, well above the MLB average of 22.0%, which is a meaningful gap for a hitter whose walk rate translates to just 9.3%. If the power carries and the strikeout rate stabilizes, he's a low-end everyday corner outfielder; if it doesn't, the profile collapses to a bench bat with a loud tool and not much else to lean on, which is exactly where ValuCast has him trending, down 15 spots in the rankings over three days.

reports.name: Wei-En Lin
reports.published_report: The WHIP is 1.0 across AAA & AA, and that's the most honest thing in this profile. Wei-En Lin is limiting baserunners at an elite clip for a 20-year-old, and his 17 walks in 53 innings translate to a 3.2 BB/9 at the MLB level, matching what an average big-league starter allows, which means the command is functional but not a separator. The strikeouts are the catch: 54 punchouts across AAA & AA sounds fine until the MLB translation comes back at 8.0 K/9, a tick below where the average MLB pitcher lands, and the whole profile hinges on whether he can generate more whiffs against better hitters than he's seeing now. If the contact management holds and the swing-and-miss ticks up, he becomes a multi-inning reliever with a useful K-BB%; if neither develops, you've got a depth arm who keeps the ball off the bases until the wrong hitter comes along.

reports.name: Aaron Ashby
reports.published_report: The Statcast profile here is elite on contact suppression and junk on command. Ashby's 32.0% strikeout rate and 2.96 xERA tell you the stuff is genuinely difficult to hit, but 11.2% walk rate is a relief pitcher walking a batter every nine batters faced, which puts a ceiling on how far the surface ERA can chase the underlying quality. The .268 xwOBA and 32.3% whiff rate are both top-shelf, and 97.3 mph off the fastball gives you the reason: this isn't deception doing the work, it's pure horsepower. If the walks stabilize even modestly, a 3.36 ERA projection starts to look conservative; if they don't, the 84.5 projected innings in a holds role still get expensive in ways a 1.37 WHIP makes pretty visible.

Hitters aren't barreling him up, they aren't hitting it hard when they do make contact, and that combination explains why his underlying numbers look like a legitimate high-leverage arm despite strikeout and chase rates that are merely average. The 12.3% walk rate is the fault line — that's a bottom-10th-percentile figure, and if the command doesn't tighten, the 3.71 ERA projection is the ceiling rather than the floor, not the other way around. Keep the contact suppression, solve the walks even partially, and he grows into a genuine setup piece for Philadelphia; let the walks stay where they are and he's a useful middle reliever who lives on the edge of trouble.

reports.name: Sterlin Thompson

reports.name: Carlos Lagrange
reports.published_report: The strikeout rate carries real weight here: 83 punchouts across 63.3 innings at AAA translates to a 9.6 K/9 at the MLB level, a full run better than what pitchers are averaging. The walk trouble is just as real — 33 free passes in that same stretch translates to a 4.2 BB/9, and that gap between his strikeout ceiling and his control floor is exactly why a near-elite punch rate produces a K-BB% that lands at barely 13.9% in MLB terms, right against the 13.5% mean. The whole profile hinges on whether he can tighten the zone enough to let the strikeout stuff breathe; if he can't, the depth-arm ceiling in his profile is the honest outcome, not a pessimistic one.

reports.name: Cal Raleigh
reports.published_report: Twelve and a half percent walks paired with a 32.0% strikeout rate tells you almost everything: Raleigh hunts a pitch he can barrel, takes his free passes, and misses a lot in between. The 12.4% barrel rate is legitimately loud, but a .175 xBA shows what happens when those barrels don't come — a lot of outs, a lot of strikeouts, and a contact floor that leaves almost no margin. The .290 xwOBA is the honest summary of a guy who provides real power in a package that hurts a lineup when the barrels aren't arriving, and the projection's .172 AVG over 518 plate appearances reflects exactly that fragility. At catcher, you tolerate this profile more readily than you would anywhere else on the diamond, but the offense lives and dies entirely on whether that 12.4% barrel rate keeps showing up.

reports.name: Felnin Celesten
reports.published_report: The surface numbers are loud for a 20-year-old shortstop at AA: .288/.381/.490 across AA & A+, with 23 stolen bases and 16 home runs in 461 plate appearances. But the translation deflates the power fast — that .202 ISO across AA & A+ becomes .143 against MLB pitching, which sits just below the MLB mean of .150, reframing the whole profile from impact bat to fringe regular at best. The strikeout concern isn't extreme at 23% across those levels, but a translated 26.2% K rate against a translated walk rate of just 9.2% means the swing decisions that look passable now get punished quickly when pitchers can locate and sequence. If the contact quality holds and the stolen base volume translates, he's a second-division everyday shortstop; if the bat speed gets exposed, what's left is a speed-and-glove bench piece with marginal on-base value.

reports.name: Alec Bohm
reports.published_report: Contact quality is genuinely there — 90.5 mph average exit velocity, a 16.3% whiff rate, a 25.5% chase rate that all point to a hitter who makes real contact with real authority. The problem is that none of it converts: a .318 xwOBA lands right at the middle of the league, and 5.8% barrels means he's hitting the ball hard without hitting it optimally, flattening the ceiling on what that exit velocity can do. The projection's .694 OPS across 626 plate appearances is the honest translation of a profile where the bat-to-ball skills are genuine but the walk rate (6.6%) is too thin to compensate for below-average power shape. He's a second-division regular if the contact profile holds at this rate; if the barrel rate doesn't climb, the walk rate probably has to, and there's no signal here that it will.

reports.name: Michael King
reports.published_report: The Statcast profile is a paradox, and ValuCast's 3.56 ERA projection is betting on the resolution. King's hard-hit rate sits at 32.4%, well below the field, and his average exit velocity of 87.3 mph reflects genuinely suppressed contact, but his xERA is 4.38 and his K% at 21.2% is ordinary, which means the soft contact isn't coming from missing bats. The walk rate at 9.6% is the problem holding the profile together wrong: he's not getting enough swings-and-misses to carry that free-pass volume, and until that tightens, the xwOBA at .322 is the more honest ledger than the ERA projection implies. If the command holds at something closer to his contact-suppression quality, he's a functional mid-rotation starter eating 184 innings; if the walks stay where they are and the weak contact regresses even a little, he's a back-end arm whose ERA drifts toward what the underlying metrics already say.

Fourteen percent across A+ & A isn't accidental patience from a teenager behind the dish, and it translates to a 10.3% MLB-equivalent rate, comfortably ahead of most big-league hitters. The contact picture is messier: his strikeout rate translates to 25.2% at the MLB level, which against a .122 MLB-equivalent ISO leaves the power profile thinner than the .178 raw ISO suggests. If the zone command he's showing with 57 walks holds and the raw power converts as he physically matures, there's a real everyday catcher here; if it doesn't, what remains is a backup with a good eye.

reports.name: Lisbel Diaz
reports.published_report: The power reads loud enough to hear from here: 24 home runs across A+ & A in 388 plate appearances, with a .255 ISO that translates to .165 at the MLB level, right around what the average big-leaguer posts. The strikeout picture is actually the easy part, 17% at his current level translating to 21.4% against a MLB average of 22.0%, so the bat-to-ball isn't the concern. The walk rate is. Four percent at A+ & A is a real problem, and a .315 OBP built on a .282 BABIP is a house of cards if pitchers ever make him prove he can take a pitch. If the discipline doesn't come, you're looking at a bench bat whose power plays in short bursts but who can't sustain a lineup role; if it does, the raw power output here suggests a lower-end regular with real run-production value.

reports.name: Robby Snelling

His K-BB% at AAA ranks 97th in the pitcher pool, and the strikeout rate translates to 9.9 per nine at the MLB level, well clear of the MLB average of 8.6. The walk rate is the one honest wrinkle: 15 free passes in 29 AAA innings translates to 3.8 per nine in the majors, a little loose for a rotation piece, and that's what the floor hinges on. If the IL stint is short and the command firms up, he's more than a depth arm; if the walks don't tighten, that depth ceiling is probably where he lands.

reports.name: A.J. Vukovich
reports.published_report: The power profile is loud at AAA, .516 slugging, .235 ISO, 9 home runs in 166 plate appearances, but the translation strips most of it away. At the MLB level that ISO comes out to .167, above average but not the weapon it looks like in the Pacific Coast League. The K% doesn't help the case: 25% at AAA translates to 24.1% against MLB pitching, above the league mean, and his 11 walks in those 166 PA leave almost no margin for contact variance to run against him. If the power travels and the strikeout rate stabilizes, he's a bench bat with real pop off the right side; if neither holds, he's organizational depth with a loud AAA stat line that didn't survive the jump.

reports.name: Christian Cairo
reports.published_report: The walk rate is the whole profile, and it's genuinely impressive — 81 walks in 441 AAA plate appearances translates to a 14.3% MLB-equivalent rate against an 8.5% MLB baseline, and the strikeout translation sits at 18.2% where most hitters are around 22%. That discipline builds a real .396 OBP at AAA, and the MLB-equivalent gets him to a respectable on-base floor even after the level discount. The problem is everything else: three home runs, a .073 ISO, and a slugging percentage that ranks in the 15th percentile of the hitter pool tell you the bat has almost no thump behind it, and the translated ISO of .087 lands well short of the .150 MLB average, a gap too wide to paper over with walks alone. Cairo becomes a useful bench piece if a team values the 24 stolen bases and the plate discipline enough to live with the near-total absence of power; if the ISO doesn't develop even modestly, he's organizational depth who happens to have excellent strike-zone judgment.

reports.published_report:
The ERA looks good. That's about where the flattery ends.

Trevor Martin is sitting on a 3.10 ERA across 43.7 innings at AAA, but the translation drains most of the intrigue: his strikeout rate moves to 8.7 K/9 at the MLB level, essentially matching what an average pitcher produces, while the walk rate comes out to 3.9 and the K-BB% lands at 12.4% against a MLB average of 13.5%. The WHIP at 1.5 and 22 walks in those 43.7 innings tell the same story the translation does — the ERA is doing him a favor that sequencing won't always grant. Everything hinges on whether he can tighten the command enough to keep hitters honest, because if he doesn't, a strikeout rate that just clears average with a below-average walk profile leaves very little margin.
